## Data: Duke lemurs

```{r}
#| echo: false

lemurs <- read_csv("data/lemurs-sample-lt24mo.csv")
```

::: midi
Today’s data contains a subset of the original Duke Lemur data set available in the [TidyTuesday GitHub repo](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/master/data/2021/2021-08-24/readme.md). This data includes information on `r nrow(lemurs)` lemurs less than 24 months old from three taxa:

- Eulemur rufus (ERUF), commonly known as Red-fronted brown lemur
- Propithecus coquereli (PCOQ), commonly known as Coquerel’s sifaka
- Varecia rubra (VRUB), commonly known as Red ruffed lemur.
:::

**We will explore the model conditions and diagnostics for a model of weight using age and taxon.**

## Univariate EDA

```{r}
#| echo: false

# univariate EDA

p1 <- ggplot(data = lemurs, aes(x = weight)) + 
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "black", binwidth = 300) + 
  labs(x = "",
       title = "Weight in grams")

p2 <- ggplot(data = lemurs, aes(x = age)) + 
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "black", binwidth = 1) + 
  labs(x = "",
       title = "Age in months")

p3 <- ggplot(data = lemurs, aes(x = taxon)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "darkcyan", color = "black") + 
  labs(x = "",
       title = "Taxon")

# bivariate EDA
p4 <- ggplot(data = lemurs, aes(x = age, y = weight)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + 
  labs(x = "Age in months",
       y = "Weight in grams", 
       title = "Weight versus Age")

p5 <- ggplot(data = lemurs, aes(x = taxon, y = weight)) + 
  geom_boxplot(fill = "darkcyan", color = "black") + 
  labs(x = "Taxon",
       y = "Weight in grams", 
       title = "Weight versus Taxon")

p1 + (p2 / p3)

```

## Fit model

```{r}
#| echo: false

lemurs_fit <- lm(weight ~ age + taxon, data = lemurs)
tidy(lemurs_fit) |> 
  kable(digits = 3)
```

# Model conditions

## Linear regression model

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \hspace{8mm} \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I})
\end{aligned}
$$

such that the errors are independent and normally distributed.

- **Independent**: Knowing the error term for one observation doesn't tell us about the error term for another observation
- **Normally distributed**: The distribution follows a particular mathematical model that is unimodal and symmetric
  - $E(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \mathbf{0}$
  - $Var(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}$

## Assumptions for regression

$$
\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{X} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I})
$$

![Image source: Introduction to the Practice of Statistics (5th ed)](images/08/regression.png){fig-align="center"}

## Assumptions for regression {.midi}

$$
\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{X} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I})
$$

1.  **Linearity:** There is a linear relationship between the response and predictor variables.
2.  **Equal variance:** The variability about the least squares line is generally constant.
3.  **Normality:** The distribution of the errors (residuals) is approximately normal.
4.  **Independence:** The errors (residuals) are independent from one another.

. . .

::: question
After fitting a model, we check a set of conditions to evaluate whether these assumptions hold for the data.
:::

## Augment data set

```{r}
#| echo: true
lemurs_aug <- augment(lemurs_fit)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

lemurs_aug |> 
  slice(1:10)
```

## Linearity {.midi}

- Examine plot of residuals versus fitted (predicted) values
- Good practice to also check plots of residuals versus quantitative predictors
- Linearity is satisfied if there is no discernible pattern in the plots (i.e., points randomly scattered around $\text{residuals} = 0$)

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 65%
#| fig-align: center


resid_v_fitted <- ggplot(data = lemurs_aug, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals versus Fitted")

resid_v_age <- ggplot(data = lemurs_aug, aes(x = age, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = "blue") + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "red") + 
  labs(title = "Residuals versus Age")
```

<br>

::: question
Why does seeing no discernible pattern mean linearity is satisfied?
:::

## Linearity {.midi}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 75%

resid_v_fitted + resid_v_age
```

. . .

::: question
Is linearity satisfied?
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: Plot made from simulated data produced by ChatGPT
#| eval: false
#| 
# code produced by chatgpt
# https://chatgpt.com/c/67bd1e0e-7650-8002-b467-1bcab2e3e172

# Simulate data where linearity is violated
set.seed(123)
n <- 100
x <- runif(n, -2, 2)
y <- x^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.8)  # Increased noise to obscure quadratic relationship

data <- tibble(x, y)

# Fit a linear model
model <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)

# Get residuals and fitted values
data <- data %>% 
  mutate(fitted = fitted(model), residuals = resid(model))

# Plot residuals vs fitted values
ggplot(data, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(subtitle = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",
       title = "Linearity not satisfied",
       x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw()



```

<!--# For multiple linear regression: if linearity is not satisfied, examine the plots of residuals versus each predictor to figure out which relationship is non-linear-->

## Equal variance {.midi}

- Examine plot of residuals versus fitted (predicted) values
- Equal variance is satisfied if the vertical spread of the points is approximately equal for all fitted values

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 50%
#| fig-align: center

lemurs_aug <- augment(lemurs_fit)

ggplot(data = lemurs_aug, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "red") + 
  labs(x = "Fitted values", 
       y = "Residuals", 
       title = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values")
```

::: question
Is equal variance satisfied?
:::

## Example: Equal variance not satisfied

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: Plot made from simulated data produced by ChatGPT
#| out-width: 75%


# simulation code from Chat gpt: 
# https://chatgpt.com/c/6987e565-b408-8327-bcfe-b1ab5049c5af

set.seed(42)

# Sample size
n <- 300

# Predictor
X <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 10)

# Heteroskedastic error:
# standard deviation increases with X
sigma <- 0.5 + 0.4 * X
epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma)

# Linear model with non-equal variance
beta_0 <- 2.0
beta_1 <- 0.5
y <- beta_0 + beta_1 * X + epsilon

# Store in a data frame
df <- data.frame(
  X = X,
  y = y,
  sigma = sigma
)

model <- lm(y ~ X, data = df)

# Get residuals and fitted values
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(fitted = fitted(model), residuals = resid(model))

# Plot residuals vs fitted values
ggplot(df, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Equal variance not satisfied",
  subtitle = "Residuals vs Fitted Values", x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw()


```

. . .

- Equal variance is critical for reliable inference. Why?

- Address violations by applying transformation on the response

## Example: Equal variance not satisfied

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 75%

ggplot(df, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Equal variance not satisfied",
       subtitle = "Residuals vs Fitted Values", x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw()

```

::: question
Is linearity satisfied in this example?
:::

## Normality {.midi}

- Look at the distribution of the residuals
- Normality is satisfied if the distribution is approximately unimodal and symmetric.
  - Even if normality is not satisfied, inference is robust for $n > 30$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out.width: 65%

ggplot(data = lemurs_aug, aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "black") + 
  labs(x = "Residuals", 
       title = "Distribution of residuals")
```

. . .

::: question
Is normality satisfied?
:::

## Normal Q-Q plot

- An alternative way to assess normality is by examining a Normal Q-Q Plot.

- The distribution of residuals is approximately normal if the points lie along the diagonal line

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(lemurs_aug, aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Residual Quantiles"
  )
```

## Independence

- We can often check the independence condition based on the context of the data and how the observations were collected.

  - If the data were collected in a particular order, examine a scatterplot of the residuals versus order in which the data were collected.

  - If data has spatial element, plot residuals on a map to examine potential spatial correlation.

- Can also check for dependence within subgroups that are not accounted for in the model

## Independence

Let's check whether there is unaccounted dependence by `sex`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
lemurs_aug <- lemurs_aug |>
  mutate(sex = lemurs$sex)

ggplot(data = lemurs_aug, aes(x = sex, y = .resid)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3)+ 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = 2) + 
  labs(x = "Sex", 
       y = "Residuals", 
       title = "Residuals versus Sex")
```

::: question
Is the independence condition satisfied?
:::

## Example of correlation over time

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: Simulation produced by ChatGPT GPT-6 Astra

set.seed(221)
n <- 150

dat <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n),
  predicted = seq(10, 30, length.out = n),
  residual = as.numeric(arima.sim(
    model = list(ar = 0.85), n = n, sd = 1
  ))
)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = predicted, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_path(color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(color = time), size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Time") +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted values",
    y = "Residuals",
    title = "Residuals with time-ordered correlation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Model diagnostics

## Model diagnostics in R {.midi}

We get observation-level model diagnostics from `augment()` in R. We will use the following columns:

- `.hat`: leverage

- `.cooksd`: Cook's distance

- `.std.resid`: standardized residuals

```{r}
#| echo: false

lemurs_aug |> slice(1:5)

```

## Influential point

An observation is **influential** if removing has a noticeable impact on the regression coefficients

```{r,echo=F}
set.seed(12)
n <- 20
x <- c(runif(n,0,1))
y <- 3*x + rnorm(n,0,.5)
new.pt <- data.frame(x=2,y=0)
x.new <- c(x,2)
y.new <- c(y,0)
data <- bind_cols(x=x.new,y=y.new)
p1<- ggplot(data=data,aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point(alpha =0.5)  + 
              geom_point(data=new.pt,color="red",size=3) + 
  geom_smooth(method="lm",se=F) + 
  labs(title = "With Influential Point")+ theme_light()+
  theme(title=element_text(hjust=0.5,size=14)) + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,2)) 

data2 <- bind_cols(x=x,y=y)
p2 <- ggplot(data=data2,aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point(alpha=0.5) + geom_smooth(method="lm",se=F) + 
  labs(title="Without Influential Point") + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 2)) + theme_light() + theme(title=element_text(hjust=0.5,size=14))  
p1 + p2
```

## Influential points

::: incremental
- Influential points have a noticeable impact on the coefficients and their standard errors
- These points can sometimes be identified in a scatterplot if there is only one predictor variable
  - This is often not the case when there are multiple predictors
- We will use measures to quantify an individual observation's influence on the regression model
  - **leverage**, **standardized residuals**, and **Cook's Distance**
:::

# Cook's Distance

## Motivating Cook's Distance

- An observation's influence on the regression line depends on

  - How close it lies to the general trend of the data

  - Its leverage

- **Cook's Distance** is a statistic that includes both of these components to measure an observation's overall impact on the model

## Cook's Distance

Cook's distance for the $i^{th}$ observation is

$$
D_i = \frac{r^2_i}{p + 1}\Big(\frac{h_{ii}}{1 - h_{ii}}\Big)
$$

where $r_i$ is the standardized residual and $h_{ii}$ is the leverage for the $i^{th}$ observation

. . .

This measure is a combination of

- How well the model fits the $i^{th}$ observation (magnitude of residuals)

- How far the $i^{th}$ observation is from the rest of the data

## Using Cook's Distance

- An observation with large value of $D_i$ is said to have a strong influence on the predicted values

- General thresholds .An observation with

  - $D_i > 0.5$ is **moderately influential**

  - $D_i > 1$ is **very influential**

## Cook's Distance

Cook's Distance is in the column `.cooksd` in the output from `augment()`

```{r}
#| echo: false

lemurs_aug |>
  mutate(obs_num = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = obs_num, y = .cooksd)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1,color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Observation number",
       y = "Cook's Distance")
```

## Comparing models {.midi}

```{r}
#| echo: false

model2 <- lemurs_aug |> 
  filter(.cooksd < max(lemurs_aug$.cooksd)) |>
  lm(weight ~ age + taxon, data = _) |>
  tidy() |>
  select(estimate)


tidy(lemurs_fit) |> 
  select(term, estimate) |>
  bind_cols(model2) |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Term", "All obs", "-Max(Cook's D)"))
```

<br>

Model coefficients do not change much because there are no influential points in the data.

# Leverage

## Leverage {.midi}

::: incremental
- Recall the **hat matrix** $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}$

- We focus on the diagonal elements

  $$
  h_{ii} = \mathbf{x}_i^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i
  $$such that $\mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_i$ is the $i^{th}$ row of $\mathbf{X}$

- $h_{ii}$ is the **leverage**: measures how far an observation’s predictor values are from the mean predictor values

  - It measures how much $\hat{y}_i$ changes when $y_i$ changes, holding the values of the predictor constant
:::

## High leverage

::: incremental
- The sum of the leverages for all points is $p + 1$, where $p$ is the number of predictors in the model . More specifically

  $$
  \sum_{i=1}^n h_{ii} = \text{rank}(\mathbf{H}) = \text{rank}(\mathbf{X}) = p+1
  $$

- The average value of leverage, $h_{ii}$, is $\bar{h} =  \frac{(p+1)}{n}$

- An observation has **high leverage** if $$h_{ii} > \frac{2(p+1)}{n}$$
:::

## Lemurs: Leverage

```{r}
h_threshold <- 2 * (3 + 1) / nrow(lemurs)
h_threshold
```

. . .

```{r}
lemurs_aug |>
  filter(.hat > h_threshold)
```

<br>

. . .

::: question
Why do you think these points have high leverage?
:::

## Let's look at the data

```{r}
#| echo: false

lemurs_aug %>%
  mutate(large_h = if_else(.hat > h_threshold, "Yes", "No"),
         large_h = factor(large_h, levels = c("Yes", "No")),
         obs_num = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = taxon, y = age)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = large_h), size = 2, alpha = 0.7) + 
  labs(x = "Taxon",
    y = "Age at weight (in months)", title = "Age vs Taxon", 
    color = "High h") +
  #theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  scale_color_viridis(discrete = T, end = 0.9)
```

## High leverage

If there is point with high leverage, ask

- ❓ Is there a data entry error?
- ❓ Is this observation within the scope of individuals for which you want to make predictions and draw conclusions?
- ❓ Is this observation impacting the estimates of the model coefficients? (Need more information!)

. . .

Just because a point has high leverage does not necessarily mean it will have a substantial impact on the regression. Therefore we need to check other measures.

# Standardized residuals

## Standardized residuals

::: incremental
- What is the best way to identify outlier points that don't fit the pattern from the regression line?

  - Look for points that have large residuals

- We can rescale residuals and put them on a common scale to more easily identify "large" residuals
:::

## Standardized residuals {.midi}

::: incremental
- The variance of the residuals is $Var(\mathbf{e}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})$

  - The variance of the $i^{th}$ residual is $Var(e_i) = \sigma^2(1 - h_{ii})$

- The **standardized residual** (also called internally studentized residual)is the residual rescaled by its variance
:::

$$
r_i = \frac{e_{i}}{\sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2(1 - h_{ii})}}
$$

## Using standardized residuals

- We can use the standardized residuals in the plot of residuals versus predicted

  - Use it to evaluate linearity, equal variance, and outliers

- An observation is a *potential outlier* if its standardized residual has magnitude greater than 3

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(data = lemurs_aug, aes(x = .fitted, y = .std.resid)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 3, color = "red", linetype =2)+
  geom_hline(yintercept = -3, color = "red", linetype = 2) +
  labs(x  = "Fitted values",
       y = "Std. Residuals",
       title = "Standardized residuals vs. fitted")
```

## Using these measures

- Standardized residuals, leverage, and Cook's Distance should all be examined together

- Examine plots of the measures to identify observations that are outliers, high leverage, and may potentially impact the model.

## What to do with outliers/influential points?

::: incremental
- First consider if the outlier is a result of a data entry error.

- If not, you may consider dropping an observation if it's an outlier in the <u>predictor</u> variables if...

  - It is meaningful to drop the observation given the context of the problem

  - You intended to build a model on a smaller range of the predictor variables. Mention this in the write up of the results and be careful to avoid extrapolation when making predictions
:::

## What to do with outliers/influential points?

::: incremental
- It is generally **not** good practice to drop observations that ar outliers in the value of the <u>response</u> variable

  - These are legitimate observations and should be in the model

  - You can try transformations or increasing the sample size by collecting more data

- A general strategy when there are influential points is to fit the model with and without the influential points and compare the outcomes
:::
